description: IoT Village at DEF CON 26 covers IoT security vulnerabilities, firmware hacking, and device exploitation. talks.title: IoT Village Keynote The Road To SOHOpelessly Broken
talks.teaser: The origins of the SOHOpelessly broken research and some of the new research from our new research lab.
talks.summary:
### The Road to SOHOpelessly Broken: IoT Village Keynote
At 00:00, Jacob Holcomb and Wick Ramgattie open the DEF CON 26 IoT Village with a keynote retrospective recounting the evolution of SOHOpelessly Broken, a landmark router hacking contest and consumer device security research initiative.

### Evolution of the IoT Village Platform
At 05:00 and 10:01, the speakers chronicle the village's rapid growth from a modest hardware hacking experiment into an internationally recognized hub for embedded systems security. They detail the systematic testing methodology developed by Independent Security Evaluators (ISE) to assess small office and home office (SOHO) network hardware.

### Vendor Collaboration and Live Exploitation
At 15:00 and 20:01, the presenters discuss bridging the gap between independent security researchers and commercial hardware manufacturers. By inviting prominent router and storage vendors (including Seagate) directly into the village, organizers created a collaborative environment where vendors could observe zero-day vulnerabilities demonstrated in real time.

### SOHOpelessly Broken 2.0: Persistent Software Flaws
At 25:10, Holcomb and Ramgattie analyze recurring architectural flaws uncovered during contest iterations. Despite years of disclosure, commercial SOHO routers and network-attached storage (NAS) devices continue to suffer from elementary programming bugs, including unauthenticated command injection, hardcoded backdoors, and broken authentication handshakes.

### Promoting Mandatory Secure Development Lifecycles
Concluding the keynote, the authors urge consumer electronics vendors to integrate automated static analysis, comprehensive third-party firmware auditing, and rapid vulnerability patching into their product lifecycles to protect consumers from widespread exploitation.

talks.title: Worms that fight back Nematodes as an antidote for IoT malware
talks.teaser: Nematodes, often called “anti-worms” or “beneficial worms”, are a controversial topic. They involve exploiting the same vulnerabilities used by malicious worms, but, rather than installing malware or being used to for...
talks.summary:
### The Concept of Defensive Nematodes in IoT Security
At 00:00, cybersecurity researcher Matt Wixey explores the controversial concept of utilizing self-propagating software worms—termed "nematodes"—as an automated defensive antidote against widespread Internet of Things (IoT) malware infections at the IoT Village.

### Historical Precedents and Legal Dilemmas
At 08:52, Wixey reviews the history of benevolent and vigilante worms, analyzing cases like the Morris Worm, Welchia, and the mysterious Hajime IoT botnet. He explores legal and ethical questions under statutes such as the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA), discussing whether unauthorized access to patch vulnerable devices can ever be legally justified.

### Autonomous Propagation and Vulnerability Discovery
At 17:44, the speaker examines autonomous spreading mechanisms across embedded platforms. He discusses proof-of-concept propagation methods, demonstrating how self-replicating scripts can traverse local wireless links, RFID environments, and open network ports to discover unpatched consumer appliances.

### Engineering Safe, Controlled Remediation Payloads
Concluding between 27:54 and 37:22, Wixey discusses technical improvements over historical anti-malware worms. He outlines design principles for non-destructive nematodes, detailing methods for reliably terminating cryptominers, patching remote execution vulnerabilities, updating default credentials, and safely de-allocating memory without bricking resource-constrained embedded devices.

talks.summary:
### Biometric Privacy in Everyday Consumer IoT
At 00:00, Erez Yalon (Checkmarx) examines the security posture of smart personal health devices, exploring how connected bathroom scales expose sensitive user biometrics and home network telemetry.

### The Proliferation of Insecure Bluetooth Appliances
At 06:00, Yalon surveys the consumer IoT market, noting that manufacturers have embedded Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) transceivers into personal devices—including smart toothbrushes, baby pacifiers, and bathroom scales—often without implementing baseline encryption.

### Reverse Engineering Smart Scale Communications
At 12:01, the presenter details reverse-engineering a commercial smart scale and its mobile companion application. The analysis reveals that the device broadcasts unencrypted telemetry payloads over standard BLE advertising packets.

### Long-Range BLE Interception and Physical Sniffing
At 18:00, Yalon demonstrates real-world sniffing tests. Utilizing standard software-defined radios and directional antennas, researchers captured unencrypted biometric data—including user weight, body fat percentages, and device identifiers—from over 100 meters away through interior building walls.

### Cloud API Vulnerabilities and Data Harvesting
Concluding between 24:00 and 30:03, Yalon highlights serious vulnerabilities in cloud backends. Companion mobile APIs frequently suffer from Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR) and misconfigured cloud buckets, allowing attackers to enumerate historical user health profiles across thousands of accounts.

talks.teaser: Many IoT devices use an ARM Cortex-M based MCU and run some kind of RTOS/"bare metal" OS. In comparison to Linux-based firmwares it is a lot more difficult to modify the firmware. If you want to change the functionali...
talks.summary:
### Dissecting ARM Cortex-M Firmware
At 00:00, embedded security researcher Dennis Giese delivers a technical guide on extracting, reverse-engineering, and modifying ARM Cortex-M firmware for smart consumer appliances at the IoT Village. Giese focuses on demonstrating practical methods for gaining local root control over connected household devices.

### Smart Device Attack Surfaces and Over-The-Air Updates
At 12:01, Giese analyzes smart lightbulb and smart appliance network architecture. He details how these devices interface with cloud servers and local mobile applications, demonstrating methods for intercepting and decrypting over-the-air (OTA) firmware update images during transit.

### Reverse-Engineering Monolithic Bare-Metal Binaries
At 23:22, the presentation breaks down the internal architecture of bare-metal microcontrollers. Unlike Linux-based IoT gateways, Cortex-M microcontrollers run single monolithic firmware binaries without filesystems. Giese demonstrates how to locate vector tables, map memory-mapped I/O peripherals, and identify core RTOS task dispatchers using disassembly tools.

### Patching Cloud Telemetry and Regional Restrictions
At 34:57, Giese demonstrates live binary patching techniques. By modifying string constants, IP addresses, and branching instructions, he alters firmware to bypass regional cloud locks, redirect telemetry to self-hosted servers, and unlock local debugging capabilities without vendor cloud mediation.

### Checksum Recalculation and Re-Flashing Workflows
Concluding between 42:00 and 47:01, Giese explains how to recalculate hardware CRC checksums and flash modified binaries back onto microcontrollers via Serial Wire Debug (SWD) and JTAG interfaces, achieving complete local control over commercial smart devices.

talks.summary:
### The Legal Minefield of IoT Vulnerability Research
At 00:00, cybersecurity legal scholar Amit Elazari guides researchers through the intricate legal statutes governing IoT device reverse engineering and security audits.

### The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and Contractual Terms
At 07:00, Elazari explores the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA). She analyzes how prosecutors and corporate vendors have historically interpreted terms of service violations as criminal "unauthorized access," weaponizing civil agreements against independent security auditors.

### DMCA Section 1201 and Anticircumvention Exemptions
At 14:01, the presentation examines Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA). Elazari reviews the legal battles led by the EFF and ACLU to secure triennial regulatory exemptions that allow good-faith security researchers to bypass digital rights management (DRM) to inspect consumer software.

### Establishing Good-Faith Research Credentials
At 21:00, the speaker details the precise criteria required to qualify for good-faith legal protection. Researchers must lawfully obtain the physical hardware, execute testing in controlled environments without disrupting production services, and refrain from weaponizing discovered flaws.

### Safe Harbor Bug Bounties and Regulatory Guidance
Concluding between 28:00 and 35:00, Elazari advocates for standardized legal Safe Harbor provisions across bug bounty programs (such as disclose.io) and highlights Department of Justice charging policy updates that protect researchers acting in the public interest.
